newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- Consumers seen driving Q4 growth in U.S.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- Consumers seen driving Q4 growth in U.S.

text.p: Consumers apparently drove a surge in U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the final quarter of 1996, according to economists polled by Reuters.
Yet few economists seemed concerned fourth-quarter growth would be forceful enough to propel Federal Reserve policy makers to ratchet interest rates higher in February.

The Commerce Department releases fourth-quarter GDP data Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters had widely varying opinions, but the average forecast saw fourth-quarter GDP growth at a 3.9 percent annual pace.
The average forecast would put fourth-quarter growth at almost double the third quarter's 2.1 percent rate.
On average, they saw the price index rising 2.2 percent versus 2.0 percent in the prior quarter, and the implicit deflator up 1.8 percent versus up 1.7 percent in the third quarter.

"We're looking for a 3.3 percent rise in GDP, with most of the strength coming from the major decline in the trade sector. We also see a surge in consumer spending on services," said Elliott Platt, director of research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
Platt also expected to see strong spending by businesses and state and local governments on new construction but no signs of strength in the housing or automobile sectors.

"The Fed may be more forward-looking and after the weak durables goods data (down 1.7 percent in December) their forecasters may have to revise downward -- by a lot -- their expectations for growth in 1997," Platt said.

He added that, based on the weak durable goods report, he expected the National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) January index to fall to 51.0 from 53.8 in December, another cause for lower growth expectations by the Fed.
The NAPM was set to release its index on Monday.
Others predicted a much stronger growth rate.

"We see a 4.6 percent rise in which the biggest area is consumption growth. Consumption will rise 3.2 percent and that category alone makes up two-thirds of GDP," said Christopher Low, senior economist HSBC Markets Inc.
He estimated business investment in construction would be up more than 20.0 percent and net exports and shrinkage of the trade deficit could contribute as much as $30 billion to GDP.
Low said 4.6 percent growth was not sustainable in 1997, but the Fed would probably focus on consumer spending.

"If early consumer spending reports come in on the high side," he said, the Federal Open Market Committee may consider raising official interest rates when it meets next on February 4 and 5. "But right now it doesn't look that way," he said. "However, they are clearly involved in a pretty open debate and there are compelling reasons to tighten."

Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc., called for "GDP growth a little higher than consensus at 4.0 percent based on an upswing in consumer spending from a 0.5 percent rise to an increase between 2.5 percent to 3.0 percent."
Leahey said a similar improvement in the trade sector would help mitigate some drag in business and car inventories.

"Once again, you have this puzzle of prices remaining stable even as wages accelerate," Leahey said of the scenario confronting Fed policymakers. "It seems that when it comes to inflation, patience remains a virtue."

"Fourth quarter GDP is probably going to be a bit of a wake-up call for the bond market. There's a lot of potential for a surprise," said Mark Vitner, economist in the capital markets group at First Union Corp.
Vitner said price cuts in clothing and electronics could be masking sales volume, meaning the holiday shopping season may have been stronger than most economists thought.

Vitner said economic news probably would continue to be strong through the release of payrolls data, then become "decidedly weaker." He saw yields on the 30-year bond peaking at about 7.0 percent in February before retreating to the trading range they have hovered in recently.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1663
